summary: Defines AES-XCBC-PRF-128, a pseudo-random function built from the Advanced Encryption Standard, for use with the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) in IPsec. It gives implementations that already have AES a way to generate key material without adding another algorithm. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A secret recipe that mixes ingredients in a scrambled but repeatable way. The two computers use it to cook up matching secret keys, built from a scrambler they already own.

questions: why does ike need a 128-bit prf
how are keys padded in aes-xcbc-prf-128
subtitle: A 128-bit pseudo-random function built from AES-XCBC-MAC by skipping its truncation step, for use in IKE.

tldr.problem: AES-XCBC-MAC outputs only 96 bits, which is too short to be a long-lived pseudo-random function in IKEv1 or IKEv2, since keys made from a 96-bit PRF are easier to attack by brute force.
tldr.mechanism: AES-XCBC-PRF-128 is AES-XCBC-MAC without the step that truncates the 128-bit value to 96 bits, and it accepts keys of any length by padding short keys with zeros and shortening long ones.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3664 and produces the same bits on the wire; the only change is that keys that are not 128 bits long are adjusted instead of rejected.

today: RFC 4434 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3664. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a 128-Bit Output
sections.content:
Some IP Security (IPsec) implementations may want a pseudo-random function (PRF) derived from the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). The existing method, AES-XCBC-MAC (RFC 3566), is a message authentication code whose output is 96 bits long. That is fine for a MAC but too short to be a long-lived PRF in either version of IKE.

Both versions of IKE use the PRF to create keys in a way that depends on the length of the PRF output. A 96-bit output creates keys that are easier to attack by brute force than a 128-bit output. The fix is very simple: omit the step that truncates the 128-bit value to 96 bits.
sections.eli5: The old recipe threw away part of the answer, which made the secret code easier to guess. The new recipe keeps all of it.

sections.title: The AES-XCBC-PRF-128 Algorithm
sections.content:
AES-XCBC-PRF-128 is identical to AES-XCBC-MAC with two changes. First, the requirement that the key be exactly 128 bits is removed, which aligns it with HMAC-SHA1 and HMAC-MD5 when those are used as PRFs in IKE. Second, the truncation step in section 4.3 of RFC 3566 is not performed, so there is no processing after section 4.2 of that document.

The key is prepared like this: a key of exactly 128 bits is used as-is; a shorter key is padded on the right with zero bits to 128 bits; a key of 129 bits or more is shortened to 128 bits by running this same algorithm with a key of 128 zero bits and the too-long key as the message.
sections.eli5: Whatever size of secret you start with, the recipe first trims or pads it to the right size. Then it mixes it up and gives you the full-size answer.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 3664
sections.content:
This document specifies the same algorithm as RFC 3664, except that the exact 128-bit key restriction is removed. Implementations of RFC 3664 produce the same bits on the wire; keys that were not 128 bits long are no longer rejected but are made 128 bits.

IKEv2 (RFC 4306) distinguishes PRFs with fixed key sizes from those with variable key sizes. Used with IKEv2, this PRF is treated as fixed-length for generating keying material but variable-length for authentication. For keying material, half the bits must come from Ni and half from Nr, taking the first bits of each. For authenticating with shared secrets, the secret does not have to be 128 bits long. The RFC admits this is somewhat tortured logic, and it lets implementations with the fixed-length semantics of RFC 3664 interoperate with implementations using the variable-length semantics here.
sections.eli5: The old rule said 'only keys of one exact size'. The new rule says 'any size is fine, we will fix it for you'. Both versions give the same answer when the size is right.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
The RFC gives three test cases, each with the same 20-byte message (000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f10111213). They exercise the three key cases: a 16-byte key, a 10-byte key that gets padded, and an 18-byte key that gets shortened.

The RFC also notes that the test vectors in RFC 3566 show the full MAC value before truncation to 96 bits, and the PRF uses that full value, so they can help verify an implementation.
sections.eli5: Test vectors are practice questions with the right answers printed in the back, so you can check that your own version of the recipe works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of AES-XCBC-MAC-PRF is based on the strengths of AES and HMAC. At the time of writing, the RFC says there are no known practical cryptographic attacks against AES, AES-XCBC-MAC-PRF or HMACs.

As with any cryptographic algorithm, part of the strength lies in the key management mechanism, the strength of the secret key and the correctness of every implementation. The RFC also asks that references to RFC 3664 be updated to refer to this document once it is published.
sections.eli5: A strong lock is only useful if the key is hard to guess and the lock is built right, so both of those still matter.
